etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English helen, from Old English hǣlan (“to heal, cure, save, greet, salute”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailijan, from Proto-Germanic *hailijaną (“to heal, make whole, save”), from Proto-Indo-European *koyl- (“safe, unharmed”). Derived from the adjective at hand in whole.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make better from a disease, wound, etc.; to revive or cure.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 8:8:
quote.text: Speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become better or healthy again.
(transitive, figurative) To reconcile, as a breach or difference; to make whole; to free from guilt.

quote.citation: 1945, United States. Congress. Senate. Committee on Foreign Relations, Global Alphabet: Hearing Before the Committee..., page 69:
quote.text: English spelling, although unphonetic and antiphonetic, was inherited from our ancestors and has served magnificently in the glorious past. The weak spot in English spelling, however, can be easily healed with the global alphabet.

definitions.definition: (roleplaying games, countable) A spell or ability that restores hit points or removes a status ailment.

quote.text: Also, various interesting spells have been added—for instance, with the Orb spell, you can circle a character, firing offensive bolts or casting heals, and free up a mage-type to cast other spells or even melee.
